page: Google Cloud Platform n2d-highmem-64 is a memory-optimized compute instance designed for large memory footprints and heavily parallelized execution. Built on the x86_64 architecture, it is powered by AMD EPYC 7B13 processors providing 64 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 32 physical cores with 2 threads per core. Cache configuration includes 32 KB L1 data cache, 0.5 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache. Vector processing support includes basic AVX, while modern vector instruction sets such as AVX-512 and AMX are not available. Hardware cryptographic acceleration is present via AES, VAES, and SHA-NI instruction sets.

The instance delivers 512.0 GB of system memory, yielding an 8.0 GB per vCPU ratio, which places it firmly in high-density memory tiers. It features no integrated local storage or hardware GPUs, necessitating remote network-attached volumes for persistent data and disk I/O. Benchmark metrics show strong multi-core processing with a stress-ng multi-core score of 86,396.78 and a PassMark CPU score of 61,717.26. Single-threaded benchmarks, such as a single-core stress-ng rating of 2,675.28 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1,522.0, fall within average percentiles, indicating an architecture optimized for aggregated throughput rather than peak single-core clock speeds.

Memory-intensive benchmarks reflect substantial capability, highlighted by cached read-only memory bandwidth of 4,074.82 GB/sec and uncached large-block write throughput of 113.39 GB/sec. Uncached large-block read bandwidth registers at an average 176.05 GB/sec. In application-focused metrics, the instance achieves strong results in database-centric operations, reaching 25,471.03 on the PassMark database test and processing 63.0 million Redis SET operations per second. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression reaches 84.97 GB/sec, while static web serving throughput measures an average 34.91 GB/sec.

Given its resource balance, Google Cloud Platform n2d-highmem-64 provides high resource density for workloads demanding high memory capacity without the overhead of dedicated GPU hardware. Tradeoffs involve relying entirely on network storage and modest single-thread capabilities. The instance is suited for in-memory databases, large Redis caches, memory-bound ETL pipelines, and high-concurrency enterprise applications.
